questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Polar Equation of a Circle Given a Point on the Circumference
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14005246/assets/abfda82949c8ed899902e142ffab0119b734d583b299e707270e293a24a9be1b.png)

Find the polar equation of the circle centered at the origin that passes through the point $A(5,2)$, as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
A circle of radius $k$ centered at the origin has the polar equation $r=k.$

We can compute the radius $k$ of our circle using the Pythagorean theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}k & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{29}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the circle is $r=\sqrt{29}.$

questions.problem: Find the Cartesian coordinates of the point where the polar curve $r=3$ intersects the negative $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
The polar curve $r=3$ is a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It crosses the negative $x$-axis at the point $(-3,0),$ as shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14005246/assets/19c6d04de928de62e63fb949cfcd770d130f8836a0bf0da06d90e7d3cb5915b2.png)

Therefore, the point of intersection is $(-3,0).$

questions.worked_solution:
The polar curve $r=3$ is a circle of radius $3$ centered at the origin. It crosses the positive $x$-axis at the point where $r=3$ and $\theta =0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14005246/assets/63d6e0d36e3d345561b1c4c20d7d19cb34ae6bd3b7543c042be288d8fcdb12e7.png)

Therefore, the point of intersection in polar coordinates is $(3,0).$
